1.pericope_label: We beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more

schools.summary: Robertson and Barnes read the opening as a transitional formula, an accusative of general reference that "does not mean actual conclusion", and both weigh the two verbs of request: Barnes finds the first weaker than the second and infers gravity from the pair — "he might have commanded them, but kind exhortation usually accomplishes more than a command." Ellicott corrects three renderings at once ("request" for beseech, "encourage" for exhort, "in" for "by the Lord"), grounding the appeal in union rather than adjuration, and finds in "the how ye ought to walk" the trace of a systematic moral code, "almost as if it were the title of a well-known book."

Calvin takes the word "abound" as evidence rather than aspiration — urging progress, Paul "intimates that they are already in the way" — and reads the choice to beseech where he might enjoin as a rule of pastoral office, "that they may, if possible, allure people to kindness, rather than violently compel them."

Clarke removes any ceiling from the command: God sets no bounds to the communications of his grace, "and as there are no bounds to the graces, so there should be none to the exercise of them", since no one can feel that he loves God or man too much.

Henry turns the phrase about walking into an aphorism — "the apostle taught them how to walk, not how to talk" — notes that those who most excel others still fall short of perfection, and draws a hard limit on apostolic authority: the apostles were commissioned to teach what Christ commanded, "not to give forth commandments of their own", nor to act as lords over God's heritage, "nor should any do so that pretend to be their successors."

Chrysostom takes "finally" as substance rather than transition, marking the turn to "things that are perpetual", and is struck that Paul does not speak of himself "as of sufficient credit to exhort" but takes Christ along with him. On abounding he builds a two-tier ethic: virtue divides into declining from evil and doing good, the first given "in the order of commandment" since doing such things brings punishment while not doing them brings no praise, the second not commanded but offered — "he that is able to receive, let him receive."

debates.question: What force does the opening word carry?

positions.view: A transitional formula, "for the rest, then", pointing towards the end without concluding
Substance, not transition: "finally" means "always and forever", marking the turn from the pressing to the perpetual

debates.question: What does "by the Lord Jesus" assert?

positions.view: Authority — Paul speaks in Christ's name, as his ambassador
Not an adjuration at all, but the ground of the request: "we encourage you, on the strength of our union in the Lord Jesus"

outliers.claim: Distinguishes commanded duties from uncommanded acts of virtue, so that to abound is to pass beyond the limit of the commandments: "as the earth ought not to bear only what is thrown upon it, so too ought the soul not to stop at those things which have been inculcated."

themes: Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more.
For ye know what commandments we gave you by the Lord Jesus.

3.pericope_label: For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication

schools.summary: Barnes forbids a decretal reading of "the will of God" — it "does not refer to the purpose or decree of God", only to what he requires — and takes the vessel of the body, since Paul directs the whole church. Robertson explains why a new word for sanctification was coined, the older term carrying "technical ideas of consecration to a god or goddess that did not include holiness in life", and inclines to the wife, drawing from it that there is "no double standard here." Ellicott argues the vessel at length for the body, turning Peter's "weaker vessel" against the marital reading and refining the sense from receptacle to instrument.

Gill takes the will of God here as decree as well as command — "in the same decree that he wills the salvation of any by Jesus Christ, he also wills their sanctification" — and declines to settle the vessel, "for the Jews call both by this name." Calvin reads sanctification as sacrifice, since "nothing can with propriety be offered to Him, but what is pure and holy", and takes the vessel of the body because Paul "addresses husbands and wives indiscriminately."

Clarke takes fornication in its widest sense, noting that manuscripts, versions and fathers add "all", leans to the wife for the vessel while forbearing to name a third interpretation, and refuses the usual comparison with beasts, since the brute creation is "regular and consistent" where the Gentiles are not.
Henry calls the body the vessel of the soul that dwells in it.

debates.question: Is "the will of God" here decree or command?

positions.view: Both, beginning with the decree of purpose in which salvation and sanctification are willed together
Command only — the text "should not be brought as a proof that God intends to make his people holy"

debates.question: What is the "vessel" each man is to possess?

positions.view: The wife, as the weaker vessel of 1 Peter 3:7 and rabbinic usage
The body, since Paul addresses the whole church and both sexes alike
Undecidable, since Jewish usage covers both

debates.question: How wide is the word rendered "fornication"?

positions.view: It includes all sorts of uncleanness — hence the addition of "all" in several manuscripts
Here it must be understood in its strict sense

outliers.claim: Explains the surprising company the prohibition keeps in the apostolic letter of Acts 15 by the novelty of the teaching: to the Gentile mind adultery's wickedness was obvious, but "it was a novelty to be told that fornication was a 'deadly sin'."

Reads the word for passion as implying "something which befalls a man, something done to him", so that indulgence is "the helpless passivity of concupiscence" — an attempted mastery that is really abandonment.

themes: For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:
That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God:

6.pericope_label: That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such

schools.summary: Barnes refuses to narrow "defraud his brother", since the Greek covers any deprivation of another's rights, in property or in marriage; keeping the reading "unto us", he takes the last verse as "a claim to inspiration". Ellicott reads the clause structurally as a final clause rather than a third parallel item — men are to be chaste "not only for their own salvation's sake, but in justice to their brethren" — dates the vengeance to the Judgment Day rather than to natural retribution, corrects "holiness" to "sanctification" as naming a process, and reads the Spirit as given "into you". Robertson supplies the papyrus sense of the avenger and notes that the verb for despising means to annul.

Gill sets aside the commercial reading, though noting that Thessalonica "was a place of great trade and business", and refers the clause to chastity. Calvin takes it of neighbourly dealing generally, dismissing Chrysostom's gloss as "too forced an exposition", and explains the vehemence of the warning by the sluggishness of mankind, who "unless they are wounded to the quick" feel no apprehension of judgment; of those who ridicule such instruction he says they "must be beaten with severe reproofs as with the stroke of a hammer."

Clarke confines the defrauding to the marriage bed, assembles the manuscript case for God giving his Spirit "unto you" rather than "unto us", and builds a distinction on it — "it is one thing to receive a revelation from the Spirit of God; it is another thing to receive that Spirit to enable a man to live according to that revelation" — the first given to the apostles alone. Wesley completes a list of three prohibitions across the passage and stops to admire the closing sentence: "what naked majesty of words!"

debates.question: What does it mean to "defraud his brother in the matter"?

positions.view: Not trade at all but chastity — adultery, or rather unnatural lust
The marriage bed: corrupting another's wife, breaking the marriage contract
Any fraud whatever; the adulterous sense is included but the Greek is not confined to it

debates.question: Did God give his Holy Spirit "unto us" or "unto you"?

positions.view: "Unto you" — the reading of many manuscripts, versions and fathers
"Unto us", making the verse a claim to apostolic inspiration
The variant is real; the choice need not be made

outliers.claim: Breaks off from exposition to praise the style of verse 8: "how oratorical, and yet with what great simplicity! — a simplicity that does not impair, but improve, the understanding to the utmost."

themes: That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.
For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness.
He therefore that despiseth, despiseth not man, but God, who hath also given unto us his holy Spirit.

9.pericope_label: But as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another

schools.summary: Barnes describes being "taught of God" as neither revelation nor inspiration but the secret teaching of providence, conscience and the Spirit, and expands the command to work into a long argument that religion "makes no one idle, and it countenances idleness in no one" — a rule which applied universally "would speedily put an end to slavery". Ellicott names the disclaimer a "sweet rhetorical figure", ranks brotherly love below charity as "to some extent the outcome of community of interests", calls the ambition to be quiet an oxymoron aimed at men who had wanted "to make a stir among the Churches", and reads the meddling as corporate rather than individual. Robertson distinguishes the New Testament sense of the word from kinship by blood.

Gill imagines a contest for "the honour of being the quietest person in the community". Calvin detaches the ambition from what follows and attaches it to love, making it "a sacred emulation" in which each strives to conquer himself, and sets the remedy for meddling in vocation, "and in this way every one keeps within his own limits."

Clarke identifies the disorder with "idle, tattling people" who "under the pretense of religion, gadded about from house to house", procuring their bread by religious gossiping, and concludes that "an idle person, though able to discourse like an angel, or pray like an apostle, cannot be a Christian."

Chrysostom explains why the chief of all good things is introduced as though passed over: the disclaimer marks the duty as too necessary to need teaching, "for things that are very important are manifest to all", and shames more effectively than admonition. He relishes the paradox — Paul "ought then to have been silent... But now by saying there is no need, he has done a greater thing, than if he had said it."

debates.question: Does the ambition of verse 11 attach to the love of verse 10 or to being quiet?

positions.view: To being quiet — an ambition deliberately paradoxical
To the love of verse 10, as a sacred emulation in which each strives to overcome himself

debates.question: Who was disturbing the peace at Thessalonica?

positions.view: Individual busybodies living off religious gossip
The whole Church, interfering ostentatiously with other Churches while its own industry suffered

outliers.claim: Paraphrases the unspoken criticism behind the compliment: "your charity is hardly catholic enough, nor have you exercised it with sufficient sobriety and thrift."

themes: But as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another.
And indeed ye do it toward all the brethren which are in all Macedonia: but we beseech you, brethren, that ye increase more and more;
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.

13.pericope_label: I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope

schools.summary: Barnes, following Koppe, proposes two causes for the grief at once — outright doubt of the resurrection and the belief that the dead would rise late and rank lower — and reads "sleep in Jesus" as cause rather than circumstance, correcting the last clause so that God brings them not down from heaven but up from their graves. Ellicott insists the sleeping is "a mere metaphor... therefore no doctrine can be deduced with precision from it", reads the participle as present so that "the grief renewed itself over each successive death-bed", and takes the prohibition of sorrow absolutely. Robertson notes the tense against the later manuscripts and cites the tombstone inscriptions for pagan hopelessness.

Gill reports the corrected pronoun from the Alexandrian copy. Calvin argues from the letter's tone that the hope had not been "torn up among the Thessalonians by profane men, as had taken place at Corinth", draws from the metaphor exactly the inference Ellicott forbids — it "refers not to the soul, but to the body", so that those who infer sleeping souls "act a foolish part" — and defends moderated mourning against Stoicism, since "it is one thing to bridle our grief... and quite another thing to harden one's self so as to be like stones."

Clarke calls the corrected reading "undoubtedly the true reading" and counts it a new discovery that the dead rise first, and so "in some measure, have the preference and advantage of such as shall then be found alive." Wesley states the temper of Christian grief most economically: Christianity "neither takes away nor embitters, but sweetly tempers, that most refined of all affections, our desire of or love to the dead."

Chrysostom denies that the ignorance was disbelief in the resurrection, since they did not disbelieve "but nevertheless bewailed", and notes Paul's method changing with the audience — at Corinth he argued from reasonings, here "he introduces nothing from reasonings, because they were docile." Verse 14 gives him his argument against those who denied the flesh: "if He did not assume Flesh, neither did He die. If He did not die, neither did He rise again."

debates.question: May Christians grieve at all for their dead?

positions.view: No: Paul "wants them not to sorrow at all over the dead", since to Christians "death ought to have no sorrows"
Yes, in moderation — the text gives no warrant for "Stoical indifference, that is, an iron hardness"

debates.question: How much doctrine may the metaphor of sleep bear?

positions.view: None with precision: it is picturesque, not doctrinal, and cannot settle whether body or soul sleeps
It refers to the body and not the soul, and those who infer that souls sleep "act a foolish part"

outliers.claim: Rejects the reading that confines "fallen asleep through Jesus" to the baptized, since "Jesus did not fall asleep through Baptism", and concludes that Paul discourses "not of a general Resurrection, but of a partial one."

themes: But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.

15.pericope_label: For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first

schools.summary: Ellicott makes "by the word of the Lord" "a most direct claim to plenary inspiration", meaning neither a citation of Christ's words nor a private revelation but "by way of a divine revelation"; he refuses to prove Paul's own expectation from the first person — "very likely he did, but it cannot be proved from this passage" — and alone reconstructs the fear, that the kingdom's highest glories would be engrossed by the living. Barnes denies an exclusive allusion to the Olivet discourse, concludes for a private communication, rescues "prevent" as meaning to precede, and surveys what little Scripture says of archangels, noting that the noun lacks the article. Robertson admits ignorance of the saying referred to and marks the strongest available Greek negative.

Gill insists the descent is personal — not by proxy, "not by the ministry of angels, as on Mount Sinai", but in soul and body. Calvin takes the opposite view of the phrase from Ellicott's, holding that it probably means what was drawn from Christ's own discourses, since "we are not the first witnesses of the resurrection, but instead of this the Master himself declared it", and reads the first person as holding all believers in suspense "that they may not promise themselves some particular time."

Clarke denies outright that the pronoun includes Paul or his readers, on the doctrinal ground that "it is impossible that a man, under so direct an influence of the Holy Spirit, should be permitted to make such a mistake"; he supplies the words of the shout — "Arise, ye dead, and come to judgment" — and lays out a nine-stage order of the day, refusing to borrow from poets "because I cannot trust to their correctness."

Chrysostom sets the formula against prophetic convention: the prophets wrote "thus saith the Lord", but Paul, "not having seen Him sitting, but having Christ speaking in himself", writes "do ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me?" — and where his other teaching came by the Spirit, this "he heard even expressly from God". Cyril of Jerusalem puts the proclamation in the archangel's mouth, "Arise to meet the Lord", and warns that "fearful will be that descent of our Master."

debates.question: What does "by the word of the Lord" claim?

positions.view: A direct claim to plenary inspiration — a message straight from God, not a citation
A private communication made to Paul by Christ
What was drawn from Christ's own recorded discourses, which would establish the point better than revelation would
Unknown: Jesus may have said it without the saying being preserved

debates.question: Does "we which are alive" show that Paul expected to survive until the Advent?

positions.view: No, and it cannot: inspiration would not have permitted such a mistake
Perhaps, but the passage cannot prove it; Paul identifies himself with his readers' expectation
The usage is pastoral, holding believers of every age in suspense

outliers.claim: Holds that the shout is not uttered by the Lord but attends him, the word being used of sailors at the oar, soldiers rushing to battle, and a huntsman calling his dogs.

themes: For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep.
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

17.pericope_label: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air

schools.summary: Barnes presses "then" to exclude "a long interval in which other important transactions would occur, such as would be involved in a long personal reign of the Redeemer on earth", analyses the seizing verb as implying external force rather than any capacity in the saints, and infers that the Lord will not descend to earth at all but remain in the air where the judgment occurs. Ellicott reads the same phrase the other way, as meaning "on the way from Heaven whence He comes... to accompany Him to His Judgment-seat on the earth", names the event "our Assumption", and prefers "in these words" to "with" in the closing exhortation. Robertson calls the rapture "a glorious climax to Paul's argument of consolation" and will not settle what follows it.

Gill enumerates the comforting doctrines — that the saints sleep in Jesus, that their bodies are his care, that they will be with him as soon as the living, and part no more. Calvin turns the promise of eternal life against millenarianism: it refutes "the reveries of Origen and of the Chiliasts", since "to assign to Christ a thousand years, so that he would afterwards cease to reign, were too horrible to be made mention of."

Clarke alone protests at the command to comfort: "comfort a man with the information that he is going to appear before the judgment-seat of God! Who can feel comfort from these words?" — answering that only the man whose sins are blotted out, or who hungers after righteousness, can. Wesley reads a division of levels, the wicked remaining beneath while the righteous, absolved, sit as assessors with their Lord.

debates.question: Where does the judgment take place?

positions.view: In the air: the Lord does not descend to earth, and "the world would not be spacious enough to contain all the assembled living and dead"
On the earth: "in the air" names the way from heaven, not a dwelling-place, and the saints accompany him to his judgment-seat below

outliers.claim: Rests the whole passage on revelation: it holds a truth "to be found in no heathen classic writer", reason having "never dared to conjecture that such scenes would occur."

themes: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
Wherefore comfort one another with these words.
